questions.prompt: What creates the floating figure in the classic Pepper’s Ghost stage illusion?
answers: An image projected onto drifting mist
A hidden figure reflected in angled glass
A costume glowing under ultraviolet light
A painted figure revealed by a rotating screen
questions.hint: The audience can look through the same surface that reflects another image.
questions.explanation: Angled transparent glass can reflect a lit figure hidden from direct view while allowing the audience to see the stage beyond. Mist projection, ultraviolet effects and rotating scenery are other theatrical techniques. Paul contrasts a present reflected view with future face-to-face knowledge; the reflection detail supports the optical connection without turning his point about incomplete knowledge into an illusion claim.
questions.authorFinding: The reading explicitly supplies reflection, so it strongly narrows the choice; the added inference is transparent glass combining two views. Test whether this is too revealing. Distinct verse from Music 1 Corinthians 13:1; context ranges do not overlap.

questions.prompt: A stage version of this scene could make Haman’s confidence funny through which device?
questions.hint: The audience has heard the king ask about Mordecai before Haman imagines his own reward.
questions.explanation: Dramatic irony creates an information gap between audience and character. The reader knows the king has been considering Mordecai’s unrewarded service while Haman assumes that the honor must be for himself. This is a narrative example of the device; Esther is not asserted to have been written as a stage play. Foreshadowing points ahead, slapstick uses physical comedy, and direct address speaks to the audience.
questions.authorFinding: The passage now supplies the example instead of the question restating the definition. The hint directs attention to the specific contrast between the king’s opening question and Haman’s assumption. It is an original paraphrase, not NIV text. Dramatic irony need not always be comic; this asks about this particular staging possibility. All paid-hint benefit remains unmeasured.

lineage.reason: Let passage supply information gap; replace generic definition and hint with scene-specific clue.

questions.prompt: Which stage musical includes the song ‘Light of the World’?
questions.hint: Its score is by Stephen Schwartz, and its scenes act out Jesus’ parables.
questions.explanation: Godspell includes this song and draws heavily on Jesus’ teaching. The reading provides its source image of visible light and good works. Jesus Christ Superstar is a different biblical musical; Pippin shares the composer but not this song; Hair is a contemporary musical with a different story. Only the song title is supplied, not lyrics.
questions.authorFinding: Direct artistic-source connection. The reading may help recognize the song, while composer plus parable-based structure separates the remaining shows. Song title contains five words; no additional song lyrics stored. Entertainment covers staged work, while Music focuses on musical structure/instruments/recordings.

questions.prompt: Which theatrical device best fits staging the rich man’s deliberation in verses 17–19?
questions.hint: Hamlet’s “To be, or not to be” is a famous example.
questions.explanation: A soliloquy gives an audience access to a character’s own thoughts through speech. The rich man works through his plans by addressing himself, which fits that device in a proposed stage adaptation. Dialogue exchanges speech between characters; a choral response comes from a group; third-person narration describes a character from outside. The surrounding parable challenges confidence in stored wealth; it is not advice endorsing his plans.
questions.authorFinding: The reading supplies who addresses whom; the stem does not restate the definition. All four choices are real presentation forms. Exclude the overlapping broader term monologue and the potentially ambiguous aside. The Hamlet example is an independent clue whose benefit is unmeasured. Vocabulary question, not a hard mechanism question. Distinct from the existing dramatic-irony example, but two theater-device questions warrant variety review.
questions.coordinatorFinding: Name/title giveaway and consecutive biblical musical after Godspell are too repetitive; replace with distinct concept.

questions.prompt: To stage the angel’s arrival in this passage, which ancient Greek theater device would fit best?
questions.hint: Picture the performer suspended in a harness.
questions.explanation: Greek theater used a crane to suspend and move a performer through the air. The angel’s descent supplies the movement to reproduce in an imagined staging. A wheeled platform reveals a scene at stage level, a scenery prism changes the backdrop, and a trapdoor lift brings a performer from below. This is a stagecraft comparison, not an explanation of the resurrection account as machinery.
questions.authorFinding: Replaces held generic thunder-sheet effect; avoids repeating guest lightning/thunder passage. Reading supplies descent without the stem saying from above. Four real stage mechanisms; choice depends on direction and function. Harness clue may be strong but does not name the device; benefit unmeasured. Ask about arrival rather than moving the tomb stone. Keep the resurrection and angel announcement context intact; no claim that Matthew describes a theatrical trick or that its narrative is a contrived plot resolution. Exact dating and reconstructions of Greek machinery vary; no dimensions or single invention date asserted. Oregon State and Utah theater handout fetched successfully. USNA403 and Chicago28MB PDF too large on direct fetch; their indexed excerpts provide harness/scenery-prism detail but full-source verification remains pending.
